questions.qtext:
Let $\Sigma=\{\mathrm{a}, \mathrm{b}, \mathrm{c}\}$. Let
$$
J=\left\{w \in \Sigma^* \mid \#_{\mathbf{a}}(w)=\#_{\mathbf{b}}(w) \text { or } \#_{\mathbf{b}}(w)=\#_{\mathbf{c}}(w)\right\}
$$
where $\#_z(w)$ is the number of appearances of the character $z$ in string $w$. For example, the word $x= \text{baccacbbcb} \in \mathrm{J}$, since $\#_{\mathrm{a}}(x)=2, \#_{\mathrm{b}}(x)=4$, and $\#_{\mathrm{c}}(x)=4$. Similarly, the word $y=\operatorname{abbccc} \notin$ $\mathrm{J}$, since $\#_{\mathrm{a}}(y)=1, \#_{\mathrm{b}}(y)=2,$ and $\#_{\mathrm{c}}(y)=3$.

Which of the following is true for $\mathrm{J}?$

Suppose we augment the DFA model by allowing each state to have one epsilon arrow. Call such an automaton an $\epsilon$-DFA. Such an automaton computes as an NFA does, but formally the transition function is of the form $\delta: Q \times \Sigma_\epsilon \rightarrow Q,$ rather than to $\mathcal{P}(\mathcal{Q})$ as in an NFA.

Which of the following is/are correct?

options.text: The language recognition power of $\varepsilon$-DFA is the same as that of DFA
The language recognition power of $\varepsilon$-DFA is the same as that of NFA.
The language recognition power of $\varepsilon$-DFA is more than DFA.
The language recognition power of $\varepsilon$-DFA is less than NFA.
